Evaluating retrieval accuracy
One of the most idx_1f9ec3f7 common misconceptions in RAG systems is assuming that a correct final
answer means the retrieval stage is working properly. In reality, the language model may
sometimes produce plausible answers even when the retrieved documents are incorrect or
irrelevant.
For this reason, it is important to evaluate the retriever independently from the language
model.
Several open tools and evaluation frameworks can help measure retrieval quality. For example,
retrieval evaluation metrics such idx_5fba2e2b as precision, recall, and hit rate can be computed using
curated test queries. A typical evaluation dataset consists of questions paired with documents
known to contain the correct answer. The retriever is then tested to determine whether those
documents appear among the top results.
Frameworks idx_f38d094b such as RAGAS (https://www.ragas.io/), DeepEval (https://github.com/
confident-ai/deepeval), and TruLens (https://github.com/truera/trulens) provide
automated ways to evaluate retrieval idx_20f50257 pipelines. These tools can measure several aspects of a
RAG idx_f4c734fd system, including:
context relevance (whether retrieved documents actually relate to the query)
answer faithfulness (whether the model answer is grounded in the retrieved context)
answer correctness compared to reference answers
As a starting point, focus on retrieval hit rate (did the correct document appear in the top-k
results?) and faithfulness (is the answer actually supported by the retrieved context). These
two metrics quickly reveal whether issues come from retrieval or generation.
A simple evaluation set can be built from real incidents: take a handful of past questions, pair
them with the log entries or documents that contain the correct answer and use them as a
reference to test whether your system retrieves and uses the right information.
For example, in our previous scenario:
"Why did the SSH service fail to start?"
The evaluation dataset would include logs containing the actual failure message. A good
retriever should consistently return the log fragment containing the error idx_904dd77f rather than
unrelated system events.
By running these tests regularly, engineers can detect problems such as poor chunking
strategies, weak embeddings, or improperly configured similarity searches.

Extending AWS compute to on-premises
environments with AWS Outposts
AWS Outposts allow idx_085e5ad6 customers to deploy cloud resources such as EC2 instances, S3 storage,
and RDS databases on-premises. These resources run on AWS-supplied physical infrastructure,
which includes racks, servers, storage, and networking equipment. All resources are managed

The physical infrastructure consists of a 42U rack, 48 inches deep, capable of housing 1U or 2U

extend your Amazon VPC from the AWS Region to your on-premises environment by defining
"Outpost subnets." These subnets provide access to VPC components such as internet

Principles that remain constant
Models, SDKs, and platforms will change, but the following engineering principles remain
useful when evaluating any generative AI capability for DevOps:
Use AI where ambiguity exists; use deterministic code where the rule is already
known. Natural-language reasoning can help interpret logs, summarize changes, or
draft artifacts. Fixed calculations, policy enforcement, and deployment gates should
remain explicit and testable.
Treat every model response as untrusted input. Do not allow fluent language or
valid-looking code to bypass the same validation standards applied to human-
authored changes.
Provide the least context and authority required. Limit repositories, files,
environments, tools, credentials, and data sources to the minimum needed for the task.
Make consequential actions observable, reversible, and attributable. Record the
initiating user or workflow, model and configuration, relevant context, tool calls,
validation results, approvals, and final disposition.
Increase autonomy only when evidence supports it. A product feature should not
receive production authority merely because a framework makes autonomous
execution easy to enable.
Memory and tools demand careful management. Each registered tool broadens an agent's
capabilities, while each memory source influences future decisions by providing additional
information. Handle both as governed interfaces: implement distinct read-only and write
functions, validate inputs and outputs, control side effects within application code, set rules
for data retention and isolation, and version tool contracts with the same deliberation as APIs.
A production readiness checklist
Before promoting an AI-assisted or agentic workflow beyond idx_b1092a4d experimentation, confirm that
the surrounding engineering system can answer each of the following questions:
Task suitability: Does the task genuinely benefit from language understanding,
synthesis, or probabilistic reasoning, or would ordinary deterministic automation be
safer and simpler?
Trusted context: Are inputs relevant, current, authorized, bounded, and classified
according to their trust level? Can untrusted issue text, logs, or pull request content
manipulate instructions?

router ospf 1

network and SW1 is on the 192.168.3.0/24 network, you would
configure it as follows:
```bash
network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 # R1's own subnet
network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 # R2's subnet
network 192.168.3.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 # SW1's subnet
```
The `0.0.0.255` is the wildcard mask that specifies which bits of
the IP address are significant for OSP

Act with approval: Permit bounded actions only after policy checks and explicit
authorization, such as rerunning a failed workflow, opening an incident, or applying a
predefined remediation.
Bounded autonomy: Automate only repetitive, low-risk actions for which the team
has accumulated sufficient evidence. Retain strict limits, audit trails, stop conditions,
rollback, and escalation paths.
Autonomy ought to be granted based on evidence. A workflow should advance to the next
stage only if evaluations, operational history, and incident reviews confirm that its existing
controls are effective.
Measure outcomes and improve continuously
Define a baseline before introducing AI, then measure whether the workflow improves the
engineering outcome rather than merely increasing model usage. Useful measures include:
Efficiency: Engineering time saved, cycle time, lead time, and time spent reviewing or
correcting generated output.
Acceptance and correction: The proportion of suggestions accepted unchanged,
accepted after modification, rejected, or escalated to a human specialist.
Quality and safety: Validation failures, test failures, security findings, false positives,
false negatives, policy violations, and escaped defects.
Reliability and performance: Latency, timeout rate, retry rate, malformed responses,
unavailable tools, and successful completion rate.
Cost: Model, compute, storage, and operational cost per successful and accepted
outcome rather than cost per request alone.
Operational impact: Changes in incident detection time, mean time to resolution,
deployment failure rate, rollback frequency, and release confidence.
Regularly review these measures and keep examples of failures and human corrections as
evaluation cases. Usage volume alone does not define success; a workflow is truly valuable only
if it enhances delivery without exceeding acceptable risk, cost, or operational limits.

Final takeaways
Before approving any new AI-enabled DevOps workflow, carry forward five questions:
Why is AI the right mechanism? Confirm that the task benefits from language
understanding or probabilistic reasoning rather than using AI where deterministic
automation would be clearer and safer.
What can the workflow access or change? Identify every context source, identity,
permission, tool, environment, and side effect before granting authority.
What evidence makes the result acceptable? Define the schemas, tests, policies,
evaluations, and approvals that must pass before the output or action is trusted.
How will the workflow stop and recover? Design timeouts, limits, safe failure
behavior, rollback, escalation, and a manual fallback before production use.
Who remains accountable? Name the owner responsible for the workflow, its
approvals, its incidents, and the consequences of what reaches production.
Generative AI assists DevOps teams in writing, summarizing, analyzing, prioritizing, and
automating tasks. However, its long-term usefulness relies on a well-structured engineering
system. Implement AI where judgment and language comprehension are critical, use
deterministic code when solutions are clear, and increase autonomy only when supported by
evidence.
Maintain every workflow as testable, observable, secure, reversible, and accountable. The goal
isn't to push engineers out of DevOps but to equip them with better tools while keeping them
responsible for what goes to production.

The type directive tells Kubernetes what kind of Secret you’re creating. In this case, type Opaque

you will see.
There are no requirements for the type directive; you can specify whatever you want if you wish to
provide your own value. That said, if you do provide one of Kubernetes’ pre-defined types, the cluster
will validate that the format matches. You can find the list of pre-defined types in Kubernetes’ Secret
documentation: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/#secret-types
For instance, if you were to set the type to kubernetes.io/tls your Secret must have a key called
tls.crt (i.e., a base64-encoded PEM encoded certificate) and a key called tls.key (i.e., a base64
encoded PEM private key), otherwise the API server will fail to create your Secret and give you an
error. Here’s an example:
$ kubectl create -f - <<EOF
heredoc> apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
name: not-tls
namespace: default
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
AD_BIND_PASSWORD: JHRhcnQxMjM=
EOF
The Secret "not-tls" is invalid:
* data[tls.crt]: Required value
* data[tls.key]: Required value
The base64 encoding of data is for a very simple reason, but is also the source of considerable confusion.
Kubernetes Secret data must be base64 encoded because secret data is often case sensitive or binary
and so must be encoded to ensure that it survives the translation from YAML -JSON -binary storage.
It’s important to understand how YAML gets stored in the Kubernetes API server to understand why.
When we work with a YAML file, the text is represented in the file by a byte (or more). This YAML is
then converted to JSON by kubectl for interacting with the Kubernetes API. The JSON that is sent to
the API server is then translated into a binary format when it is stored. The problem we run into with
many text-based formats is that there are multiple ways to represent text-based data in a binary format.
For instance, UTF-8, which is one of the most common encodings, can use from one to four bytes to
represent a certain character. UTF-16 uses one to four 16-bit “code units”. ASCII can only encode the
English alphabet, Arabic numerals, and common English punctuation. If the encoding from YAML –
JSON - binary and back involves switches encoding types, data can be lost or corrupted.

Threats to Secrets at Rest
When a secret, such as a credential or a key, is in storage it is referred to being “at rest,” since data is
not being moved. Nearly every compliance framework requires that secrets at rest be encrypted. This
makes sense; why wouldn’t you encrypt your data at rest? In Kubernetes, you can configure etcd to
encrypt data at rest and you may think you’ve not only met a compliance requirement (often referred to
as “checking the box”) but increased the security of your cluster! The truth is much more complicated.
Before we dive into how Kubernetes encrypts data at rest, let’s do a quick recap of how encryption
works. All encryption involves three basic components:
• Data: Either encrypted (cipher text) or decrypted (plain text).
• Key:Used to encrypt your plain text to cipher text and to decrypt your cipher text to plain text.
• Algorithm: Some process to combine the key and data to encrypt or decrypt it.
Every encryption class or book will teach you that the key is always a secret while hiding the algorithm
should never be relied upon for secrecy. This means that if an attacker knows you’re using AES-256, it
really doesn’t matter because it’s the key that’s the secret.
What’s important here is that if you’re using encryption, you must have a key available to encrypt and
decrypt the data. There is a great deal of nuance in how the different algorithms work, differences
between block and stream ciphers, how keys are generated, etc. That nuance isn’t important to this
discussion, no matter how fascinating it is. The fact that you need your key and data in the same place
at the same time limits the security impact of encrypting data at rest because the security is only
increased if the data and the key are separate.
With that sidebar in encryption completed, you might start to see the issue with encrypting data in
Kubernetes’ database. Kubernetes does support encrypting data and we’re not going to cover it here
because of the complexities, other than to describe it at a high level.
Kubernetes encryption works by configuring an EncryptionConfiguration object that identifies what
data is encrypted and with what keys. This object is accessible from the host running your API servers.
Do you see the flaw with this? If someone has access to the cluster, they have the keys!
If your etcd instances are run on different servers there’s some additional security, but does that
benefit offset the risks involved when you need to decrypt and re-encrypt for key rotation? That’s a
decision you need to make on your own.
Does encrypting your data at rest make your clusters less secure? Consider the “ CIA triad of security”
that’s most often used to describe the security requirements and impacts on a system. CIA stands for:
• Confidentiality: Can we ensure we’re the only ones who have access to this data?

of availability going down due to key rotation is much reduced, making this a much easier decision.
If encrypting data in transit increases security, is it compliant? This is where we get the opposite of
the “data at rest” scenario. From a technical perspective, a certificate authority is easy to build. Back
before we had cert-manager or Kubernetes, I built a simple API-based CA for a customer that wanted
to lock down APIs from a mobile app using Java and the openssl command. Building a compliant CA
is much harder. It often involves volumes of management and regulations. For this reason, while most
large enterprises have an internal CA that could be used, you can’t use it from within Kubernetes. If
your cluster doesn’t match all the rules of your CA, it invalidates the compliance of those rules and
breaks your compliance.
The compromise that is often struck is for your ingress controller to have a wildcard certificate while
an internal CA is used for communications within a cluster.
There is a strong argument that the increase in automation overcomes the introduced weakness of
an in-cluster key for a CA, but as compliance is often a legal requirement those arguments generally
fail. This is why it’s so important to understand the difference between security and compliance. In
these two use cases we’ve shown how they conflict and why you need to understand those conflicts
to make design choices.
Having walked through how to encrypt secret data in transit, the last scenario to explore is secrets
when they’re used in your applications.
Protecting Secrets in Your Applications
Let’s walk through a potential, and all too common, scenario. You’ve built a “secure” cluster. Your
secret data is all stored in a well-designed secrets manager. You’re following all the guidance on how
to manage that data. Every connection is encrypted. Your application loads, gets a password, and
connects to a database. It turns out that two years ago someone found a flaw in your parsing library
that lets an attacker open a shell on your app and get access to that password and since you need to
talk to that database they can connect and extract all the data!
What went wrong? Going back to the previous two scenarios, we established multiple times that you
must have the secret in hand to use it. This means that if your application has a security flaw, it doesn’t
matter how well designed your secrets management process is, it becomes the weakest link.
This doesn’t mean we should abandon secrets management. Supply chain security is its own focus
and one we will cover later in this book. The point is that when you consider how to build your secrets

Podman accepts both unqualified and fully qualified images. The difference is quite simple
and can be illustrated as follows:
A fully qualified image includes a registry server FQDN, namespace, image name, and
tag. For example, docker.io/library/nginx:latest is a fully qualified image. It has a
full name that cannot be confused with any other Nginx image.
An unqualified image only includes the image's name. For example, the nginx image

result from the basic podman search nginx command will not be official and should be
analyzed in detail to ensure they're trusted. The output can be filtered by the OFFICIAL
flag and by the number of stars (more is better).
The first global setting of the registries configuration file is the unqualified-search-registry
array, which defines the search list of registries for unqualified images. When the user runs the
podman search <image_name> command, Podman will search across the registries defined in
this list.
By removing a registry idx_e102b4df from the list, Podman will stop searching the registry. However,
Podman will still be able to pull a fully qualified image from a foreign registry.

_namespace_…]/repo(:_tag|@digest) pattern, though simpler patterns, such as

If a Kubernetes Secret is fine, why are we bothering with secrets managers at all? There are two
reasons: compliance and GitOps.
From a compliance perspective, most compliance frameworks require that you not only know when
secret data changes, but also when it’s used. For instance, NIST-800-53 requires that you continuously
monitor the usage of credentials (which makes up the bulk of secret data). While you could set up
logging in Kubernetes to track this, it makes it much easier to audit by having it in a central location.
The next reason why we should evaluate a secrets manager is GitOps. In the last two chapters, we’re
going to explore GitOps, a large part of which is storing our configuration in a Git repository. You
should never, ever, EVER, EVER, EVER store secret data in a Git repository either in plain text or as
encrypted data. Git repositories are designed to be easily forked. Once forked, you’ve lost control of
that repository. Going back to compliance, this is a big risk as you have no way of knowing if a devel-
oper forked your internal repository and accidentally pushed it to a public GitHub repository. There
are other reasons why keeping secrets in Git should be considered an anti-pattern, but we’ll cover that
when we talk about sealed secrets. Using a secrets manager allows us to externalize our secret data
from our cluster, even though Secret objects are most likely fine for most clusters.
Having looked at why regular Kubernetes Secrets are usually fine from a security standpoint, let’s
look at what sealed secrets are and why they’re an anti-pattern.
Sealed Secrets
If you are externalizing your Kubernets manifests into a Git repository, you may be tempted to store
sensitive secret data there too. You don’t want anyone to get that data though, so you decide to encrypt it.
Now, however, you need to decrypt it to get it back into your clusters. Bitnami (now owned by VMware)
released a tool called Sealed Secrets (https://github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets) that does
just this. You install the operator into your cluster and when it sees a SealedSecret, it decrypts it for you.
This seems like a simple and elegant solution for externalizing secret data securely. Unfortunately, its
apparent simplicity is what leads to this solution being an anti-pattern.
The first issue with Sealed Secrets is that secret data is stored in Git. We pointed out in the previous
section that this is a bad idea from a security perspective. One of the main goals of secrets manage-
ment is being able to track the usage of secrets. It’s incredibly easy for a developer to push an internal
repository to a public service like GitHub or GitLab. Take this simple command line:

sys.exit(0)

self.wfile.write(message)

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, signal_handler)

Running Docker Engine inside a container is generally not recommended due to several reasons, including security,
stability, and potential performance issues. This practice is often referred to as Docker-in-Docker or DinD. The i d x _ 1 2 d 7 2 5 a b
main concerns are as follows:
Security: Running Docker Engine inside a container requires elevated privileges, such as running the
container in privileged mode or mounting the Docker socket. This can expose the host system to
potential security risks, as a compromised container could gain control over the host's Docker daemon
and escalate privileges, affecting other containers and the host itself.
Stability: Containers are designed to be isolated, lightweight, and ephemeral. Running Docker Engine
inside a container can create complex dependencies and increase the chances of conflicts or failures,
particularly when managing storage, networking, and process namespaces between the host and the
nested container environment.
Performance: Running Docker Engine inside a container can introduce performance overhead as it adds
another layer of virtualization, particularly in terms of storage and networking. This can lead to
increased latency and reduced throughput, particularly when managing large numbers of containers or
when working with high-performance applications.
Resource management: DinD i d x _ 2 e 8 8 0 a 8 0 can make it challenging to manage and allocate resources effectively, as
nested containers may not inherit resource limits and restrictions from their parent container, leading to
potential resource contention or over-commitment on the host.

There are four ways that a workload can consume secret data:
• Volume mounts: Similar to reading a file from a PersistentVolumeClaim, secrets can be mount-
ed to a pod and be accessed as a file. This approach can be used with both external secrets
and with Secret objects. This is generally the preferred approach when working with security
teams. If a Secret is updated while a pod is running, the volume will eventually get updated,
though this can take some time based on your Kubernetes distribution.
• Environment variables: Secret data can be injected into environment variables and consumed
from the workload like any other environment variable. This is often referred to as “insecure”
since it’s a common practice for application developers to dump environment variables for
debugging purposes. It’s not an uncommon occurrence for debugging components to be ac-
cidently kept in production that are leaking environment variables. It’s better to avoid this
approach if possible. It’s important to note that if a Secret is updated while a pod is running,
the environment variable in the running pod is not updated.
• Secrets API: Kubernetes is an API and Secrets can be accessed directly via the Secret API.
This approach provides more flexibility than either environment variables or volume mounts,
but requires knowledge of how to call the API. If you need to be able to dynamically retrieve
Secrets, this is a good approach but is probably overkill for most applications.
• Vault API: Every external vault provides an API. While we’re using tools like External Secrets
Operator or a sidecar to interact with these APIs, there’s nothing stopping a developer from
calling these APIs on their own. It would cut down on the external configuration, but at the
cost of tightly binding your system to a particular project or vendor.
Next, we’re going to walk through these options to see how they’re implemented.
Volume Mounts
The preferred way to add Secrets to your workloads is to treat them as files and load them into your
application. This approach has multiple advantages over the other approaches listed above:
• Less likely to be leaked during debugging: There’s nothing that stops a developer from print-
ing the contents of a file to the logs or an output stream, but a call to the env command won’t
automatically print out secret data.
• Can be updated: When a file is updated, that update is reflected in your pod. The same is true
for secret data that is mounted via a volume. If the application in your pod knows to look for
updates, it will eventually get them.
• Richer options: A configuration file mounted onto a volume can be more than name/value
pairs. It can be full configuration files, simplifying management.
Mounting a secret as a volume has been a feature of Kubernetes since Secrets were available. In this

A database of information i d x _ c 6 3 2 f 0 a 9 security problems that have been made publicly known is called Common
Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A number uniquely identifies each vulnerability from a list of all other entries in
the database. This list is continuously reviewed and updated by experts who include any new vulnerabilities or
exposures as soon as they are found.
Now, we can scan the various layers of our Docker images using specialist software, such as Snyk, to find software
libraries that are known to have such CVEs. If we find that our image is flawed, we should and can repair the issue
by switching to a more recent version of the flawed library. The image will then need to be rebuilt.
But our work is not yet done. Security experts frequently find new CVEs, as was already mentioned previously. As a
result, a software library that was previously secure may suddenly be vulnerable as a result of a newly revealed
i d x _ a 8 b e 3 c d 9 CVE.
This means that we must ensure that all of our active Docker images are routinely inspected, notify our developers
and security experts about the issue, and take other steps to ensure a speedy resolution of the issue.
There are a few ways to scan a Docker image for i d x _ 4 6 f 0 2 d 6 1 vulnerabilities and i d x _ a 7 e d 4 6 3 5 secrets:
Use a vulnerability scanner such as Clair, Anchore, or Trivy. These tools can scan a Docker image and
check it against a database of known vulnerabilities in order to identify any potential security risks.
Use a tool such as AquaSec or Sysdig to scan the image for secrets. These tools can detect and alert on
sensitive information such as private keys, passwords, and other sensitive data that may have been
accidentally committed to the image.
Use a combination of both tools, for example, Docker Bench for Security, which checks for dozens of
common best practices around deploying Docker containers in production.
Use a tool such as OpenSCAP that can perform vulnerability scans, security configuration assessments,
and compliance checks on a Docker image.
It's important to note that it's always good practice to keep your images updated and only use official and trusted
images.

To implement multi-tier applications, such as those with a frontend, middleware, and a
backend, the best practice is to create and orchestrate multiple containers, each one running a
specific component. The goal is to have minimal and very specialized containers, each one
running its own service/process while following idx_c6b3d1c4 the Keep It Simple, Stupid (KISS)
philosophy, which has been carried out in UNIX systems since their inception.
Despite being great for most use cases, this approach does not always suit some special
scenarios where many processes need to be orchestrated together. An example is when we
need to share all the container namespaces across processes, or when we just want a single,
uber image.
Container images are normally created without an init system, and the process that's executed
inside the container (invoked by the CMD instruction) usually idx_e34ad062 gets PID 1.
For this reason, Red Hat introduced the UBI Init image, which runs a minimal systemd init
process inside the container, allowing multiple systemd idx_da1de8bc units that are governed by the systemd
process with a PID of 1 to be executed.
The UBI Init image is slightly smaller than the Standard image but has more packages available
than the Minimal image.
The default CMD is set to /sbin/init, which corresponds to the systemd process. systemd
ignores the SIGTERM and SIGKILL signals, which are used by Podman to stop running
containers. For this reason, the image is configured to send SIGRTMIN+3 signals for termination
by passing the STOPSIGNAL SIGRTMIN+3 instruction inside the image Dockerfile.
The following example shows a Dockerfile/Containerfile that installs the httpd package and
configures a systemd unit idx_c9696057 to run the httpd service:

yum clean all && \
systemctl enable httpd
RUN echo "Successful Web Server Test" > /var/www/html/index.html
RUN mkdir /etc/systemd/system/httpd.service.d/ && \
echo -e '[Service]\nRestart=always' > /etc/systemd/system/
httpd.service.d/httpd.conf

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is a service that enables
organizations to idx_f812f14c manage, control and monitor access to important resources like Microsoft
Entra ID, Azure and other Microsoft Online services like Microsoft Intune and Microsoft 365.
PIM provides time-based and approval-based role activation that minimizes the risk of
excessive, unnecessary or misused access permissions on resources.
Organizations want to restrict the number of users that have privileged access to prevent a bad
actor from getting that access or an authorized user inadvertently or maliciously misusing the
access. However, IT admins still need privileges to carry out privileged operations in Microsoft
idx_cc922016 Entra ID, Azure or Microsoft 365. Using PIM organizations can give admins just-in-time access
to resources and oversee what they are doing with that access.

It provides just-in-time access to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources
It provides time-bound access to resources
It can require approval to activate privileged roles
It can enforce MFA to activate privileged roles
It can ask for justification to activate the privileged role
Access reviews can be conducted to ensure users still need the roles
Notifications can be sent when privileged roles are activated
Audit history is maintained for internal or external audits

Environment Variables
Using environment variables is the easiest way to consume any data. Every language and platform
has a standard way to access an environment variable. The downside to this ease of access is that it’s
common for developers to print out or dump all their environment variables for debugging. This means
that the data could end up in a log, or even worse a debugging webpage that prints out environment
variables. This mechanism will often be flagged by security teams, so it should be avoided if possible.
That said, some workloads require environment variables, so let’s look at how to integrate both plain
Kubernetes Secrets and secrets from our external Vault into a pod.
Using Kubernetes Secrets
Kubernetes can plug a Secret object’s data directly into an environment variable inside of the Pod
definition of the container. Here’s a simple example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
labels:
run: test
name: test-envvars-secrets
namespace: my-ext-secret
spec:
containers:
- image: busybox
name: test
resources: {}
command:
- env
env:
- name: MY_SECRET_PASSWORD
valueFrom:
secretKeyRef:
name: secret-to-be-created
key: somepassword
dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
restartPolicy: Never
Looking at .spec.containers[name=test].env, you can see that we create an environment variable
from an existing Secret. The command of this container is simply the env command, which prints
out all the environment variables. To see this container in action, apply the YAML from the chapter8/
integration/envvars/envars-secrets.yaml:
$ cd chapter8/integration/envvars
$ kubectl create -f ./envars-secrets.yaml

The Vault sidecar doesn’t support injecting environment variables directly, because sidecar images

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
labels:
run: watch-vault-env
name: test-envvars-vault-watch
namespace: my-ext-secret
annotations:
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
vault.hashicorp.com/log-level: trace
vault.hashicorp.com/role: extsecret
vault.hashicorp.com/tls-skip-verify: "true"
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-myenv: 'secret/data/extsecret/
config'
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-myenv: |
{{- with secret "secret/data/extsecret/config" -}}
export MY_SECRET_PASSWORD="{{ index .Data "some-password" }}"
{{- end }}
spec:
containers:
- image: ubuntu:22.04
name: test
resources: {}
command:
- bash
- -c
- 'echo "sleeping 5 seconds"; sleep 5;source /vault/secrets/myenv ; env |
grep MY_SECRET_PASSWORD'
dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
restartPolicy: Never
serviceAccountName: ext-secret-vault
serviceAccount: ext-secret-vault

to retrieve Secrets. The good news is that you’re not really doing anything different for the Secrets
API than any other API. Most of the Kubernetes client SDKs even handle base64 decoding the data
from Secret objects.
Since this isn’t a programming book, and there are many ways to interact with the API, we’re not going
to dive into any SDK specifics. We’re going to cover some specific guidance:
• Use Your Pod’s Identity: Just like interacting with external vaults, use your Pod’s own identity
when interacting with the API server. Don’t use a hardcoded Secret.
• Use an SDK: This is good general advice. Yes, you can use the Kubernetes API via a direct REST-
ful call, but let the SDK do the work for you. It will make life easier and lead to fewer security
issues (who hasn’t accidently logged a token while testing an HTTPS call? I mean, besides me).
• Store Metadata in CRDs: Any situation where you’re going to describe a secret should be done
in a CRD. This gives you the benefit of having a schema language that you can use to generate
your own SDKs.
While it is more difficult to interact with the Secrets API than to use Kubernetes’ multiple abstrac-
tions for interacting with secrets, it does provide tremendous flexibility that is not available to the
more common abstractions. Next, we’ll look at whether interacting directly with our vault’s API can
provide the same benefits.
Using the Vault API
Every vault service has an API. That’s how the sidecars that integrate with them interact with their
vaults so that they can inject secrets into your workloads. In the previous section, we walked through
the advantages of directly calling the Kubernetes Secrets API. Does the same logic apply to the Vault
API? The reasoning for calling the Vault API, or any secrets management API, directly is the same as
calling the Secrets API.
What are the disadvantages of calling the Vault API directly? The main drawback is that you are now
tightly binding your workload to a specific vendor or project. One of the benefits of the Kubernetes
API is that it is relatively consistent across implementations. While this isn’t always true, at least for
the Secret API it is.
There is unfortunately no standard API for secrets, nor is there likely to ever be one. HashiCorp, AWS,
Microsoft, Google, VMWare, etc. all have their own ideas as to how secrets should be managed and
there isn’t much incentive to create a standard. There’s also no standard for integrating language bind-
ings. For instance, the database world often has common standards for integrating into programming
languages such as the JDBC standard in Java. It would be great for Kubernetes to make the Secrets
API pluggable, but that will never happen. The complexities at both the technical and non-technical

Plan PIM deployment
Planning a PIM deployment is a critical step for organizations aiming to enhance their security
posture and idx_986e0984 manage access to sensitive resources effectively. Without thorough planning,
organizations may face challenges in assigning the correct roles, ensuring compliance, and
maintaining visibility over privileged activities. A well-conceived deployment plan helps
identify which roles require PIM, ensures that all licensing requirements are met, and
establishes clear processes for approval and activation workflows. This preparation not only
minimizes the risk of unauthorized access but also streamlines the user experience for those
who legitimately need elevated privileges.
Furthermore, planning allows organizations to align PIM implementation with broader IT
governance and compliance objectives. By mapping out business needs, regulatory
requirements, and operational processes beforehand, organizations can configure PIM settings
—such as approval requirements, notification policies, and auditing mechanisms—in a way
that supports both security and productivity. It also provides an opportunity to educate
stakeholders about the new processes, reducing confusion and resistance during rollout. A
strategic approach to PIM deployment ensures that privileged access is granted only when
necessary, for the right duration, and under proper oversight, thereby reducing the attack
surface and supporting ongoing risk management efforts.
It is recommended idx_8d2e57bb to start with a pilot which will consist of a small set of test users to ensure

roles, Azure roles, and groups. This should include members of a group, members of a role, IT

can verify that all configuration is set up correctly and move to production with confidence.

educate them on how their experience will change and how they can get support if required. It
is also important to have a rollback plan in place in case PIM fails to work as desired.

on code structure, rules, semantics, and analysis reports. Because these two testing approaches
have different workflows and pain points, this section examines them separately, beginning with
dynamic testing and then moving to static testing.

testing works and where its practical limitations arise.

(6) Performance testing
The main objective of performance testing is to evaluate the system’s speed, response time, and
resource usage. By designing and implementing a series of test scenarios, performance testing
helps identify and analyze the system’s behavior under various loads. This type of test focuses
on key performance indicators such as throughput, response time, CPU, and memory usage,
aiming to optimize system efficiency and ensure strong performance in real-world environments
to meet user needs. Performance testing effectively reveals performance bottlenecks in the system
and provides a basis for corresponding optimization and improvement.
(7) Security testing
The main objective of security testing is to discover and eliminate security vulnerabilities in the
system to ensure the safety of data and resources. By simulating various possible attack methods
and analyzing the system’s protection mechanisms, security testing evaluates the system’s ability
and robustness in resisting malicious attacks. This type of test covers potential security threats
such as authentication, authorization control, data protection, and network security. Through
security testing, potential security issues can be identified, security measures can be strengthened,
and the system’s integrity and confidentiality of data and resources can be effectively safeguarded
in the face of security challenges.
(8) Compatibility testing
The main objective of compatibility testing is to verify the software’s compatibility across a
variety of different environments (including operating systems, browsers, devices, etc.). By
testing the software on diverse software and hardware configurations and network environments,
it ensures consistency and stability across different platforms and devices. Such testing covers
compatibility across operating system versions, browser types and versions, mobile and desktop
devices, and even performance under different network conditions. Through compatibility testing,
environment-specific compatibility issues can be discovered, ensuring that the software meets
the needs of a broad user base regardless of their technical conditions.
(9) User interface testing
The main objective of User Interface Testing (UI Testing) is to verify the functionality and
appearance of the software’s user interface, ensuring a high-quality and consistent user
experience. By thoroughly testing the interactivity, layout, response speed, and visual consistency
of various interface elements, it can be confirmed whether they function correctly and comply
with design specifications. Such testing includes the functional behavior of buttons, text boxes,
menus, icons, dialogs, etc., as well as how the interface appears on different resolutions, window
sizes, and devices.

TestGen-LLM workflow overview
TestGen-LLM leverages static code analysis and the comprehension capabilities of LLMs to deeply
analyze the structure and logic of existing Kotlin test cases, identifying potentially missed test
paths, such as edge cases, abnormal situations, or specific code paths. Static analysis techniques
help to understand code structure and dependencies, while LLMs can capture the semantics and
intent of test cases, learning code styles and patterns.
Based on the analysis of existing test cases, TestGen-LLM can use the generative power of LLMs
to automatically generate new test cases. According to the structure and logic of the code, as well
as the needs of the testing team, it can design test cases covering more scenarios. Meanwhile,
TestGen-LLM also references existing test cases, learning their style and patterns to ensure
the generated test cases are consistent with the existing test code style, making them easy to
understand and maintain.
To ensure the generated test cases can be used directly and effectively improve test coverage,
TestGen-LLM performs a series of filtering and validation steps. First, it checks whether the
generated test cases can be successfully built to avoid compilation errors. Then, it executes the
test cases and verifies whether they pass, guaranteeing that the test cases can correctly validate
the specific behavior of the code. Next, it repeatedly runs the test cases to ensure that they do not
exhibit instability, such as passing under certain conditions and failing under others. Finally, it
checks whether the test cases improve test coverage, ensuring that previously missed scenarios
are now covered.

Applying LLMs in Software Testing 284
Intelligent evolution of static testing
After examining dynamic testing, the discussion now turns to static testing, where software is
analyzed without being executed. Static testing plays a different role in the quality-assurance
process: instead of observing runtime behavior, it examines code structure, rules, dependencies,
semantics, and potential vulnerabilities before the software runs. This makes it especially useful for
early defect detection, but it also introduces challenges such as false positives, rule maintenance,
and difficulty interpreting complex code.
Basic concepts of static testing techniques
In addition to dynamic testing techniques, static analysis is another fundamental method in
software testing. Static testing detects potential issues and defects by analyzing the software
code without actually running the program. Since static analysis can be carried out in the early
stages of software development, it has unique advantages in identifying errors, vulnerabilities,
and bad practices in the code. The key steps of static analysis are shown in Figure 8.5.
Figure 8.5: Key steps of static analysis
1. Code Review Preparation: Testers need to prepare the codebase to be analyzed, ensuring
its completeness and correctness, and configure the relevant static analysis tools. The code
review preparation stage may also involve preprocessing steps such as code formatting
and comment cleanup, in order to improve the accuracy and readability of the analysis.
In this chapter, “static testing” refers specifically to automated static analysis tech -
niques; manual reviews and walkthroughs are out of scope.

Use case: AI-driven scaling for performance and cost
After reaching out to experts across the industry, one idx_a47e6ae3 common thread we found was that AI is
being leveraged significantly for scaling use cases.
Types of scaling
There are two types of scaling in computing: vertical and horizontal. Vertical scaling is the
process idx_537a7a3e of scaling up in place. In other words, expanding or reducing the size of a disk, adding
CPU or memory to a virtual machine, and so on. Horizontal scaling is the process of adding or
removing an additional copy of the resource you're measuring. That could be another set of
Pods, another Kubernetes node, another virtual machine, or another load balancer, as
examples. However you choose to scale, your scaling strategy needs to be intentional and tied
to the business needs.
Scaling for performance
Scaling for idx_b60f03d9 performance means keeping the system resources balanced so that applications are
as performant as possible. Imagine a basic queue. You can set a threshold that, if exceeded,
then another thread pool is created to work through the queue items. In most cases, for scaling,
simple automation does the trick; however, that automation is typically reactive. With AI
available to parse large amounts of data and identify possible patterns, you can go from
reactive to proactive. For example, financial institutions may notice a sharp uptick in traffic as
the stock markets open on Monday mornings. Agentic systems can proactively scale
environments up a little ahead of this spike, so that price information, trade information, or
any other type of system interaction is always as fast as possible. If traffic patterns change, the
agentic system will detect these new patterns and adjust accordingly, as opposed to a human
operator regularly tracking these patterns and updating automated thresholds.

2. Selection of Static Analysis Tools: The effectiveness of static analysis tools is closely
related to the programming language used by developers, the project scale, and specific
requirements. Common static analysis tools include SonarQube, Pylint, ESLint, FindBugs,
etc. These tools can automatically scan code, identify potential issues, and generate
detailed reports. Choosing the right tool is key to successful static analysis, as different
tools vary in their detection capabilities and performance.
3. Defining Rules and Standards: Before performing static analysis, a set of code quality
rules and standards needs to be defined. These rules usually cover coding conventions,
naming conventions, security checks, performance optimization recommendations, and
so on. By clearly defining the rules, the consistency and reliability of the analysis results
can be ensured. Many static analysis tools provide predefined rule sets and also allow
users to customize rules to meet specific needs.
4. Executing Static Analysis: After preparation is complete, testers use the selected tools
to perform static analysis on the codebase. The tools scan the code, apply the predefined
rules, identify potential issues, and generate reports. The execution of static analysis is
usually automated, but in some cases, manual intervention may be required to handle
complex code structures or specific business logic.
5. Result Analysis and Reporting: The reports generated by static analysis tools contain
issues found in the code, including errors, warnings, and suggestions. Testers must
analyze these results in detail to determine which issues actually need to be addressed.
The result analysis phase also involves determining priorities so that the development
team can focus on the most important issues. Static analysis reports not only help identify
code defects but also provide concrete suggestions for improving code quality.
6. Issue Fixing and Verification: Based on the static analysis results, the development team
needs to fix the code. After the fixes are completed, the static analysis tool is usually run
again to verify whether the issues have been resolved. This process may require multiple
iterations until all critical issues are resolved. Through repeated static analysis and fixing,
the code quality and reliability can be significantly improved.

throughout the development lifecycle, static analysis should be integrated into the

Complexity analysis
The main goal of complexity analysis is to assess the complexity of code, including loop
complexity, conditional complexity, and coupling between modules. By analyzing code
complexity, high-complexity areas that may be difficult to maintain and test can be identified,
guiding the development team to refactor and optimize code. Complexity analysis is relatively
common in embedded industries where software runtime resources are limited.
Dependency analysis
The primary goal of dependency analysis is to examine the dependencies between code modules
to ensure that module coupling remains within a controllable range. By analyzing dependencies,
issues such as circular dependencies and unused dependencies can be identified, thereby
optimizing code structure and improving the maintainability and scalability of the system. At
the same time, dependency analysis can also identify security issues introduced by dependencies
by comparing with third-party vulnerability databases and similar data sources.
Although these techniques can detect many issues early and operate efficiently across large
codebases, static testing still faces important limitations in real production environments.

Compared to dynamic testing techniques, static testing techniques demonstrate significant
advantages in code coverage, operating costs, and concurrency efficiency. However, when applying
static analysis tools in actual production environments, there are still many pain points and
challenges. These challenges not only affect the practical effectiveness of the tools but also impose
higher demands on the workflows of development teams.

positives, meaning the reported problems do not actually exist. A high false positive rate
not only increases the extra workload for developers but may also diminish their trust
in the analysis results, thereby affecting the tool’s practical effectiveness. Frequent false
positives force teams to spend more time filtering true errors from false positives, gradually
eroding developers’ enthusiasm for and trust in static analysis.

You may not realize it but Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a very complex field of AI. Nat -
ural language is inherently ambiguous—it includes humor, irony, homonyms, polysemy, and
more. Even among humans, miscommunication is common. We often need to repeat ourselves
or clarify our intent by providing additional context.
The most challenging aspect of NLP is capturing semantics—that is, understanding the meaning
of words within their specific context. In traditional AI, we rely on techniques such as tokenization.
Tokens can represent entire words, subwords, or even individual characters such as punctuation
marks. AI models are trained on tokenized text and automatically break down our inputs into
tokens during processing. Tokenization is a fundamental technique used by every NLP practitioner.
However, tokens alone are not enough to extract semantics. A very popular NLP technique used to
extract semantics is Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging. This technique involves identifying words and
their grammatical roles within a sentence, and it remains relevant today. While tokens represent
individual, context-free segments of text, tags provide a more comprehensive understanding by
revealing the grammatical structure of the sentence.
For example, take the following sentence:

The corresponding tags would be as follows:
"I" - Pronoun (PRP)
"am" - Verb (VBP)
"Stephane" - Noun (NNP)
"Eyskens" - Noun (NNP)
"," - Punctuation (",")
"an" - Determiner (DT)
"Azure" - Adjective (JJ)
"Cloud" - Noun (NN)
"Architect" - Noun (NN)
. (period) - Punctuation (PUNCT)
Once we have identified each word and its grammatical role in a sentence, we gain a deeper un -
derstanding of the text. Punctuation also plays a crucial role—symbols such as ., !, and ? help
indicate sentence boundaries, questions, and emphasis. POS tagging is often performed using
stochastic methods such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), which excel at predicting the most
likely sequence of letters, words, tags, or phonemes based on transition probabilities.

Addressing challenges in deploying LLMs for testing
This section provides an in-depth discussion of the application potential of LLMs in dynamic
software testing and static software testing. It demonstrates their powerful logical reasoning
capabilities, natural language processing skills, code generation abilities, and how they can
enhance the effectiveness and accuracy of traditional software testing techniques. Without a
doubt, LLMs show broad application prospects in the field of software testing. However, when we
attempt to apply LLMs in real-world software production environments, we still face numerous
complex technical difficulties and challenges. This section, drawing on practical experience in
deploying LLMs, will delve into these technical challenges.
Model reliability challenges
Before LLMs can be used reliably in testing workflows, teams must understand the core limitations
that affect model output, especially context window constraints and hallucinations.
Managing LLM context window limits
Currently, LLMs generally have limitations on the context input window when processing text
data. For example, GPT-4’s context input window is capped at 32,000 tokens. Although some
foundational LLMs claim to handle ultra-long contexts, their ability to “find a needle in a haystack”
and “maintain focused attention” in the face of massive amounts of data still requires further
validation. As a result, in software testing scenarios, LLMs may encounter insufficient input
window issues when analyzing longer code fragments or test data, making it difficult for the
model to directly address complex testing requirements and results.
A feasible solution is to use other analytical techniques to segment and structure the data before
feeding it to the LLM, and then input the data into the model step-by-step via RAG or Agent
technologies. This approach can effectively alleviate the limitations of the processing window
and enhance adaptability to complex tasks. For example, splitting code by functional modules
and then incrementally inputting them into the LLM for analysis can help improve processing
efficiency and accuracy.
Reducing hallucinations in testing workflows
Since the emergence of LLMs, they have often been plagued by the issue of “ hallucination.”
When LLMs handle problems with frequent context switching, complex logical reasoning, and
a large amount of mathematical computation, they frequently provide irrelevant answers or fail
to understand the logic of the question. This phenomenon results in an inability to fully trust the
output of LLMs when using them to assist in software testing. Currently, it remains technically
difficult to completely resolve this issue at the foundational level.

Best practices for PIM
The following are some best practices that help organizations get the most value out of PIM:
Enforce Just-in-Time access: Convert all standing privileged assignments into eligible
roles. This reduces the attack surface and aligns with Zero-Trust by ensuring admin
rights exist only when needed.
Require MFA for activation: Make MFA mandatory for every privileged activation.
This blocks compromised credentials from being used to elevate access.
Use approval workflows for high-impact roles: Roles such as Global Administrator,
Privileged Role Administrator, and User Administrator should require explicit approval
before activation.

Require justification for every activation: Require business justification for each

Enable alerts for suspicious or excessive activations: Monitor unusual patterns such

Selecting the right foundation model
LLM technology is developing rapidly, and foundation models with different numbers of
parameters and various pre-training tasks are emerging one after another. Models ranging from
1 billion to 200 billion parameters exhibit varying inference performance and efficiency depending
on the task. In software testing tasks, choosing the most suitable model to achieve the best results
at the lowest computing cost is particularly important. For example, for integration testing of
complex systems, selecting a large-parameter model may yield better inference performance, while
for simple unit testing, a smaller-parameter model can be chosen to save computing resources.
In addition, some enterprises have strict data security management mechanisms and do not
allow core data (such as code) to be sent to the cloud for processing. In such cases, it is necessary
to consider the feasibility of deploying LLMs locally, balancing computing power and cost while
ensuring data security. For example, a localized and streamlined LLM can be deployed and
combined with the enterprise’s own data security strategies, thereby better protecting data
privacy and security.
After selecting a suitable base model, teams must decide whether the model’s existing capabilities
are sufficient or whether fine-tuning is needed for testing-specific tasks.
Deciding whether to fine-tune LLMs
Fine-tuning LLMs is an effective way to significantly improve their performance on specific
reasoning tasks. Experiments show that fine-tuned LLMs demonstrate obvious enhancements
in tasks such as code explanation and program repair. However, as the base models develop,
their parameter counts, and the scale of training corpora increase rapidly—models with up to
100 billion parameters considerably raise the cost of fine-tuning. In addition, these base models
already cover most common corpora during pre-training, including code, and software testing-
related data, so the performance improvement from fine-tuning may gradually diminish.
Therefore, whether to fine-tune a base model and whether it is cost-effective requires a
comprehensive trade-off based on the situation. For example, when handling common code review
tasks, one may choose not to fine-tune but instead directly leverage the pre-trained capabilities
of LLMs; however, when working on testing tasks in specific domains, proper fine-tuning can
significantly boost performance.
Improving model performance is only one part of deployment. In testing workflows, teams also
need to understand why a model produced a recommendation and whether testers, developers,
and security teams can trust the result.

conventional static code analysis but also conducts more detailed data modeling of the source
code. When generating vulnerability reports, Corax stores contextual information related to each
vulnerability in a database. This data includes the code snippets triggering the vulnerabilities,
involved functions and variables, and related configuration file information. The purpose of this
is to reference this detailed information during subsequent prompt engineering, significantly
reducing potential hallucinations by the LLM, thus improving the accuracy of vulnerability repair.
Once the vulnerability and its relevant code context have been localized, the next step is to package
that information into a prompt that the LLM can use to generate a repair.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 302
Generating LLM prompt
After the user selects the vulnerabilities to be automatically repaired, Corax aggregates all data
required for repairing those vulnerabilities. This data covers detailed vulnerability information,
relevant code snippets, code context information, and associated knowledge from the security
vulnerability knowledge base. This data serves as the RAG query results, entering the next step
of prompt engineering. The LLM will systematically organize this data according to a preset
format, including the user’s specific requirements and questions, then send it to the underlying
LLM interface. The key in this step is to ensure that the input information provided to the LLM is
comprehensive and accurate, enabling it to generate high-quality repair suggestions.
After the LLM generates a repair suggestion, the system must convert the output into a form that
developers can inspect, verify, and apply safely.
Processing model output
After the LLM generates repair suggestions, Corax continues to process these outputs. First, Corax
converts the repair code generated by the LLM into natural language explanations, including an
analysis of the vulnerability’s cause and a detailed description of the repair strategy. This step
not only helps developers understand the root cause of the vulnerability and the repair method,
but also verifies the correctness of the repair code produced by the LLM. Next, Corax converts the
repair code returned by the LLM into more practical formats, such as code diff or git pull/request,

Model context protocol
As of June 2025, MCP remains an emerging pattern and is highly subject to change in the future,
but the philosophy behind it should remain the same.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 310
As noted in the previous section, implementing the TAG pattern at scale can be challenging, since
an AI application may need to interface with numerous services, each with its own quirks. This
complexity becomes difficult to manage.
MCP partially addresses this challenge by defining a standardized way to describe features and
tools. Each tool can implement its own MCP server, while each consuming service maintains
its own set of MCP clients. These clients and servers communicate using a common protocol,
ensuring consistent interaction patterns.
At this stage, the relationship between each client and server is one to one. The MCP server acts
as an abstraction layer over the underlying remote service—such as a database or an API—and
encapsulates the logic required to interact with that service.
The application remains the orchestrator between the LLM and its set of MCP resources. However,
it no longer needs to implement custom, ad hoc interactions for each individual service and can in -
stead rely on MCP to standardize those interactions. Figure 8.11 provides a high-level view of MCP:
Figure 8.11 – High-level view of an MCP-enabled application

In Figure 8.11, the application uses its various MCP clients to retrieve metadata about the tools
and resources exposed by their corresponding MCP servers. At this stage of MCP adoption, most
AI solutions host both MCP clients and servers themselves. This approach is primarily driven by
security concerns, as full trust in MCP—particularly from a security standpoint—has not yet
been established.
Typically, service owners develop the MCP server and distribute it as a container image or a
package that can be integrated with different AI solutions.
An MCP server will typically expose at least the following operations:
@server.list_tools()
@server.list_prompts()
@server.call_tool()
@server.get_prompt()
These operations allow clients to fetch information and call the tools exposed by the server.
While running a local MCP server is appropriate for accessing local resources, it becomes less
suitable for interacting with remote resources exposed by remote services.

Next, let’s explore agentic AI.
Agentic AI
Agentic AI goes beyond being a simple design pattern—it encompasses any autonomous AI system
capable of making decisions and performing tasks without human intervention. For instance, an
agent could independently book a hotel room by evaluating factors such as price, comfort, and
availability. A key characteristic of agentic AI is the ability of agents to tackle complex tasks, which
requires them to reason and formulate a plan to achieve the desired outcome.
An example of a complex task could be the autonomous planning of a technical intervention
of a malfunctioning fridge in a retail store (see the smart fridge monitoring in retail stores use
case in Chapter 7), detected by a monitoring system. The agent would be triggered by the alert.
It should be able to find the most appropriate technician, check availability, and so on. It would
take multiple steps and important coordination to make this possible.
However, to achieve this, the agent would most probably leverage a few of the patterns we have
learned about so far, such as RAG (knowledge), persist state, TAG (tooling), and MCP (context
and tooling), to augment the agent’s capabilities. An agent might rely on other agents to make a
decision. This is called multi-agent orchestration. The context, tooling, reasoning, and knowledge
can be added using low-code or pro-code solutions.
If you’re just getting started with agentic AI, the Copilot Studio portal is an excellent entry point.
It offers a low-code approach that makes it easier to grasp the principles behind agentic AI and
achieve meaningful results without the complexity of building everything from scratch.
Copilot Studio integrates seamlessly with the broader Microsoft ecosystem, enabling you to
build event-driven agents that can respond to specific triggers—such as receiving an email or
the creation of a SharePoint document. You can also schedule agent activities using the recurrence
trigger type, allowing agents to run at predefined intervals.

VPN overlap
One common place to encounter IP addressing overlaps is when helping users through VPN connec -
tion troubleshooting. Many businesses allow employees to bring a laptop home and create a VPN
connection from their house into the corporate network, so that they can access company resources
from home. If the user’s home router assigns their laptop an IP address in the 192.168.1.x range, and
there is also a network inside the business network that is 192.168.1.x, what happens? Things get
messy is what happens, where sometimes that user may be able to access information over the VPN,
sometimes not at all, and sometimes only certain servers and not others. These variables depend on
the configuration and capabilities of the platform providing your VPN, but ultimately, the only way
you will truly help that employee to have a normal, successful VPN connection is if you walk them
through changing their entire home network to no longer run on 192.168.1.x, but something entirely
different, perhaps 192.168.100.x or even 10.10.10.x.
So many home-class routers default to using 192.168.0.x or 192.168.1.x IP addresses that any net -
work admin worth their salt should know to never configure a business network to utilize either of
these IP addressing ranges.

Subnet mask
Referring back to Figure 8.1, the next piece of information we must populate for a successful network
connection is the subnet mask. In almost all home networks, you might find your IP address to be
something like 192.168.1.100. This is your full IP address, but what isn’t immediately obvious is that
only the last portion (.100) is your individual workstation identifier on the network. The rest of that
address (192.168.1) is known as a network address. In IPv4-land, the way that IP addressing works
is that each of those four octets can contain a number from 0 through 255. You can define whether
more of your IP addresses should be dedicated to network addressing, or to host/device addressing.
There are three classes of IPv4 subnets, and each one has advantages/disadvantages because they
allow either more separated networks within your environment, or more host addresses within each
network. Let me break it down this way, by looking at a few different subnet mask options:
• Class A subnet = 255.0.0.0 = 128 different networks, each with 16,777,216 hosts

Chapter 8 339
Since we are now using a /16 subnet, that means the entire latter half of the IP address is dedicated
to host addressing, and so even though 192.168.1.x and 192.168.128.x seem like they are very far
apart, within a /16 network, these two sets of IP addresses (and everything in between) are all part of
the same network. In this scenario, your two test computers would be able to talk to each other just fine.
Public subnetting
Our information so far all pertains to internal networks and private IP addressing, but the same math
and mechanisms exist on the public internet. When purchasing internet service for a business, or
even your home, a common question from the ISP is whether you want any static IP addresses to be
part of your service. If you say yes, they will ask how many you need. The entire internet plays by the
same IPv4 rules we have been discussing here, and so available and usable IPv4 addresses on the in -
ternet are limited. It is very common for companies to be given a very small set of usable IP addresses,
maybe five or perhaps even one. The way that ISPs control the distribution of these tiny amounts of IP
addresses is by dedicating even more of the IP address to be network identification, thereby causing
less of the IP address to be usable for host addressing. When dealing with public IP addressing, it is
common to see CIDRs and subnet masks such as the following:
• 255.255.255.252 (/30) = 2 usable IP addresses (1 for you to use)
• 255.255.255.248 (/29) = 6 usable IP addresses (5 for you to use)
• 255.255.255.240 (/28) = 14 usable IP addresses
…and so on.
If you ever need to remind yourself of these numbers, or figure out what subnet sizing is appropriate

As with any computer system, ensuring that it’s secure and that only authorized users access
the system is paramount. Security should be incorporated at the beginning of your application
design and not as an afterthought. AWS provides a broad set of security offerings that assist in
keeping your applications secure and your data protected. Notice that we used the word assist.
Just because you are using AWS does not mean that your applications will be instantly secure.
Here is a quick example of how easy it is to expose your data: There is nothing barring you from
creating a bucket in AWS that is both unencrypted and public. You may get some warnings ask -
ing you whether you are certain that you want to proceed, but AWS won’t disallow it. You could
then put a client file in that bucket that may contain emails, passwords, names, addresses, and
so on. This combination would immediately make this data accessible to anyone in the world
with an internet connection (including any threat actors). However, S3 public access is blocked
by default from AWS.
Even though you may not have published the URL for the bucket, please don’t assume it is se -
cure. Threat actors know these mistakes happen sometimes. They constantly send requests to
random Amazon S3 buckets, trying to guess whether they were created unsecured and exposed.
And occasionally, they get lucky and hit pay dirt.
In the following section, we will learn more about what security AWS provides without involv -
ing the user and what services and tools AWS provides to its users to keep their systems secure.
Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model
AWS uses the Shared Responsibility Model, which means that AWS and its users are responsi -
ble for keeping applications secure. However, the lines of responsibility are pretty clear. AWS is
solely responsible for some aspects (for example, physical data center security), and users are
solely responsible for other aspects (for example, making sure that Amazon S3 buckets that will
contain sensitive information are private, accessible to only authorized users, and encrypted).
This model enables AWS to reduce the burden of securing some components needed to create appli -
cations while enabling users to customize the applications to suit their clients’ needs and budgets.
Depending on the service chosen, some responsibilities may fall on AWS or the user. For example,
if you use Amazon RDS to stand up an instance of MySQL, the patching of the database and the
underlying operating system would be performed by AWS.
Suppose you instead decide to install MySQL directly into an Amazon EC2 instance. In that case,
you will still be able to use the MySQL functionality. But in this case, the responsibility to patch
the operating system and the database would fall on you.

Ping traffic is technically called ICMP traffic. This is important because the ICMP protocol is blocked
by default more and more often these days, with firewalls being turned on by default on so many of our
systems and devices. Historically, ping was always a tool that we could count on to tell us with a fair
degree of certainty whether connectivity was flowing between two devices, but that is no longer the case.
If you build a brand-new Windows box and plug it into your network, that computer may communicate
with the internet and all of the servers on your network just fine, but if you try to ping that new computer
from another machine on your network, the ping will probably fail. Why would that happen? Because
Windows has some security measures built into it by default, including blocking ICMP traffic in Windows
Defender Firewall. In that case, you would need to either turn off the Windows firewall or provide it with
an access rule that allows ICMP traffic. Once such a rule is enabled, pings will start replying from this
new computer. Keep in mind, whenever building new systems or servers in your network, that ping is
not always the most trustworthy tool to depend upon in today’s security-focused world.
It’s easy to allow ICMP responses by plugging a rule into Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced
Security, though you still wouldn’t want to have to remember to do this manually on every new system
you introduce into a network. Thankfully, you already know how to utilize Group Policy to build a GPO
and push it out to all machines on your network, and yes, you can absolutely place firewall rules inside
that GPO. In fact, we will do exactly this in Chapter 10, Hardening and Security. This is a common way
to allow or block ICMP throughout an entire organization, by issuing a firewall rule via Group Policy.

The Windows routing table
When you hear the term routing table, it is easy to pass that off as something the network folks need
to deal with, something that is configured within the network routers and firewalls. It doesn’t apply
to server admins, right? Networking servers together has been made easy for us by only requiring an
IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway, and we can instantly communicate with everything
inside the rest of our network.
While there is indeed a lot of networking magic going on under the hood that has been provided to
us by networking equipment and network administrators, it is important to understand how routing
inside Windows works because there will be some cases when we need to modify or build out a routing
table directly on a Windows server.
Multi-homed servers
Running multi-homed servers is a case where you would certainly need to understand and work with
a local Windows routing table, so let’s start here. If you think this doesn’t apply to you because you’ve
never heard of “multi-homed” before, think again. Multi-homed is just a funny-looking word meaning
your server has more than one NIC. This could certainly be the case for you, even if you are a small
shop that doesn’t have a lot of servers. Often, small businesses or essential servers have multiple
network interfaces, separating internal LAN traffic from internet traffic. Another instance of a multi-
homed server would be a remote access server that provides DirectAccess, VPN, or proxy capabilities

at the edge of your network. Yet another reason to be interested in and understand multi-homing is
Hyper-V servers. It is very common for Hyper-V servers to make use of multiple NICs because the VMs
that run on that server might need to tap into different physical networks within your organization.
Now that we have established what a multi-homed server is, you might still be wondering why we are
discussing this. If we have more than one NIC, don’t we simply configure each NIC individually inside
Windows, giving each one an IP address, just like we would for any NIC on any server? Yes and no.
Yes, we configure a distinct IP address on each NIC, because it needs that for the identification and
transport of packets on the network. No, we do not set up all of the NICs on your server in the same
way. There is one critical item that we need to keep in mind and adhere to in order to make traffic
flow properly on our multi-homed server.

Building a route
So, what is our answer to all of this? Building a static routing table. When you have multiple NICs on a
server, thereby making it multi-homed, you must tell Windows which NIC to use for what traffic inside
the routing table. This way, when network traffic needs to leave the server for a particular destination,
the routing table is aware of the different directions and paths that the traffic will need to take in order
to get there and will send it out accordingly. You will still rely on routers to take the traffic the rest
of the way, but getting the packets to the correct router by sending them out via the proper physical
NIC is key to making sure that traffic flows quickly and appropriately from your multi-homed server.

NIC teaming
Moving on to another network topic that is becoming more and more popular on server hardware, let’s
walk through the steps to create NIC teaming. The ability to team NICs essentially consists of binding
two or more physical network interfaces together so that they behave as if they were a single network
interface within Windows. This allows you to plug two physical cables into two different switch ports,
all using the same settings. That way, if one NIC port, switch port, or patch cable goes bad, the server
continues working and communicating without hesitation, because teaming allows the NIC that is
still working to handle the network traffic.
NIC teaming itself is nothing new. It has been around for more than 10 years inside the Windows Server oper -
ating system. However, early versions were problematic, and in the field, I find that Server 2019 is the earliest
server operating system most IT personnel consider to be stable enough to use NIC teaming in production.

on your server. I currently have four NIC ports on this machine. I have plans to create two teams: my
first and second NICs will be bound together to become an internal network team, and my third and
fourth NICs will become a DMZ network team. This way, I have network card redundancy on both
sides of my network flow on this server.

A few things to be clear about at the outset are:

modules and device drivers.
